events.title: Spanish conquest and New Granada
hints: Spaniards searched for a gilded king and a lost city of gold in the 1530s.
The Muisca highlands were conquered in 1537-1539, and a viceroyalty was created in 1717.
Enslaved Africans worked gold mines in the west and in Cartagena's slave port.
events.summary: Santa Marta was founded in 1525, and Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada conquered the Muisca in 1537-1539. Spain governed the region as the New Kingdom of Granada and, from 1717, a viceroyalty. Gold mines depended on enslaved Africans, and Cartagena was a major slave port.

events.title: Spanish reconquest and the Reign of Terror
hints: After a 1810 declaration, a large expeditionary army under Pablo Morillo arrived to restore the crown.
Cartagena was starved in a long siege, and many revolutionaries were executed.
Simón Bolívar's victory at Boyacá in August 1819 ended the occupation.
events.summary: In 1815 Spain sent about 10,000 troops under Pablo Morillo to restore royal rule. After a long siege of Cartagena and executions of revolutionary leaders in 1816, the occupation ended with Simón Bolívar's victory at Boyacá in 1819.

events.title: US-backed separation of Panama
hints: After the national senate rejected a canal treaty in 1903, a northern power backed a secessionist movement in the isthmus.
US warships blocked troop landings, and recognition came within days.
Roosevelt later said, "I took the Isthmus."
events.summary: When the senate rejected the Hay-Herrán Treaty in 1903, the United States supported Panamanian separatists, sent warships to prevent Colombian troop landings and recognised the new republic within days. Colombia received a 25 million dollar indemnity under the 1921 Thomson-Urrutia Treaty.
events.quip: Theodore Roosevelt's own summary: "I took the Isthmus."

events.title: Banana massacre
hints: Workers on fruit plantations near the Caribbean coast struck in late 1928 for written contracts and safer conditions.
Troops were sent after the company lobbied the government.
Soldiers fired on strikers and families in a railway-town plaza in December.
events.summary: In late 1928 about 25,000 workers struck against the United Fruit Company at Ciénaga, seeking written contracts and better conditions. On 6 December soldiers fired into a crowd in the plaza at Ciénaga. The number of dead is disputed, with estimates from dozens to over a thousand.
